title: Ketchup Was Once Sold as Medicine 💊🍅 #shorts
description:
In 1834, American doctor John Cook Bennett claimed tomatoes could treat diarrhea, indigestion and liver trouble – and recommended tomato ketchup as a remedy. By 1837 he had teamed up with Archibald Miles to sell "tomato pills", sparking a craze full of rival pill makers. Some of those pills didn't even contain tomatoes, and by around 1850 the fad was gone.

Sources: Mental Floss, Atlas Obscura, JSTOR Daily, Chowhound, The Daily Meal, Andrew F. Smith (The Tomato in America)

scenes.headline:
KETCHUP WAS
MEDICINE

scenes.text: In eighteen thirty four, an American doctor named John Cook Bennett made a bold claim about tomatoes.
He said they could treat diarrhea, indigestion and liver trouble. And he recommended tomato ketchup as a remedy.
By eighteen thirty seven, he teamed up with a businessman named Archibald Miles to sell tomato pills.
It became a craze. Rival doctors sold their own pills, and they fought each other in the newspapers.
The twist? Some of these tomato pills didn't contain any tomato at all. A few were just laxatives.
The whole craze lasted only about sixteen years. By around eighteen fifty, it was over.
scenes.label: OF TOMATO PILL HYPE

scenes.text: But Americans kept the ketchup. Today it's on fries everywhere, no prescription needed.
